body:
## What

When a definite-length CBOR array opens and the input is contiguous, the reader now reads the integers, floats, booleans and nulls that follow in one tight loop (`parse_cbor_scalar_run`). It switches on the head byte, loads the big-endian value straight from the input buffer and calls the SAX handler. Elements no longer go one by one through `parse_cbor_internal`'s container bookkeeping and `parse_cbor_value`'s dispatch.

- The loop stops at any other kind of value (strings, containers, tags, half floats, simple values) and when fewer than 9 bytes are left. Those values go through the existing path, which reads them exactly as before, so positions, errors and SAX events do not change.
- It runs only once, when the array opens. A check in the main loop, run for every element, cost +3 % on citm_catalog, whose arrays mix scalars and objects.
- Non-contiguous inputs (streams, `std::list` iterators) are not affected. Tag dispatch on the bulk-scan capability means they never instantiate the bulk calls.
- `number_float` now receives a member empty `string_t` as its source, instead of a `std::string` constructed for every float.

This is the CBOR part of the binary-format research (see #5968 for the BSON part).

## Measurements

Instructions and time per parse, B/A (A = develop 755bb16d7a), from the ab-harness one-binary A/B (both layouts). The Mac is an M1 Max with Apple clang (instructions retired, 60 reps); GCC 13 is x86-64 under callgrind.

| | Mac instr | Mac time | GCC 13 instr |
|---|---|---|---|
| SAX canada | 0.523 | **0.471** | 0.854 |
| DOM read canada | 0.909 | 0.926 | 0.935 |
| SAX citm_catalog | 0.989 | 0.985 | 1.008 |
| DOM read citm_catalog | 0.998 | 0.993 | 1.001 |
| SAX twitter | 0.999 | 0.999 | 1.006 |
| DOM read twitter | 0.999 | 0.995 | 0.998 |
| strict UTF-8, citm_catalog | 0.998 | 0.991 | 1.001 |
| `std::istringstream`, citm_catalog | 0.999 | 0.992 | 1.006 |

Canada is mostly arrays of doubles; citm_catalog and twitter mix scalars with strings and objects. No row is more than 1 % worse.

Two more changes were tried and left out because each made GCC's stream path (`input_stream_adapter`) 0.5–4 % worse through inlining changes:
- a `memcpy` + `bit_ops::byteswap` `byte_swap` for floats (another −3.5 % on GCC DOM read canada);
- taking the container frame by reference in `parse_cbor_internal`.

## Tests

New test case "CBOR arrays of scalars from contiguous and non-contiguous input" in `unit-cbor.cpp`. It reads a document containing every scalar head the loop handles, among them the 1/2/4/8-byte integers, −2^64 as a float, int64 min, half/single/double floats, booleans and null. It checks values and then, for every truncation of the document, compares contiguous against non-contiguous input:
- the result or error of `from_cbor`,
- the full SAX event log,
- a SAX handler that stops after each of the first 60 events.

The full ctest suite passes with ASan/UBSan (184/184).

## Update: review commit

The second commit removes the `cbor_scalar_follows()` pre-check, since `parse_cbor_scalar_run` returns on the same conditions anyway, and sets the value size explicitly in every case. Measured against the first commit:

| B/A | GCC 13 instr | Mac instr |
|---|---|---|
| SAX canada | **0.915** | 0.914 |
| DOM read canada | 0.990 | 0.988 |
| SAX citm_catalog | 1.003 | 1.004 |
| DOM read citm_catalog | – | 1.002 |
| SAX twitter | 1.000 | 1.001 |
| `std::istringstream`, citm_catalog | 1.000 | – |

The table above is for the first commit alone. With both commits, SAX canada is about 0.78 (GCC) and 0.48 (Mac) of develop's instruction count.

## Breaking changes

None. Values, error messages, error positions and SAX events are unchanged. The public API is untouched.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

review_comments.body: explicit `size = 1` in all cases that rely on the default, so that it's obviously intentional?  Could maybe then leave `size` uninit to remove a duplicate store in the other cases?

Why is this function needed?  Calling `parse_cbor_scalar_run` will immediately return false exactly on these conditions.  The only thing this avoids is the `container_stack.back()`.  Is that expensive enough that calls to `bulk_remaining()`, `bulk_data()` and a test of `head` are far less expensive?

## Flawfinder / Does not check for buffer overflows when copying to destination (CWE-120).

buffer/memcpy:Does not check for buffer overflows when copying to destination (CWE-120).

[Show more details](https://github.com/nlohmann/json/security/code-scanning/1109)

Done in 43665e5. `size` is now left uninitialised, and every case that relied on the default (`false`/`true`/`null` and the one-byte integers) sets `size = 1` itself. The bail-out branch never reads it. gcc and clang give no uninitialised-variable warnings at -O0 to -O3, and the instruction counts are unchanged.

With callgrind on synthetic CBOR shaped like citm_catalog, canada and string/object arrays (I could not download the real files here), the pre-check saved about 0.2-0.6 % of instructions on arrays that start with a non-scalar and cost about 0.8 % on arrays of numbers, so it was a wash. I have not re-run the real citm_catalog and canada timings; the CI benchmarks will show whether the numbers in the description still hold.

A correction to my reply above: after it, 8bbfb5ec1d put `cbor_scalar_follows()` back, and I didn't say so here, sorry. Your question on #5980 made me measure it again, and it's now gone for good in `b43555493b`. `enter_cbor_array` calls `parse_cbor_array_start` directly, and `parse_cbor_scalar_run` is a `while` loop that checks the remaining count and length first. MessagePack in #5980 now works the same way.

Instructions per repetition, measured in one binary, new/old:

| case | clang (Mac) | GCC 13 (Linux, callgrind) |
|---|---|---|
| SAX twitter | 1.000 | 1.001 |
| SAX citm_catalog | 1.002 | 1.004 |
| SAX canada | 0.983 | 1.002 |
| read twitter | 1.000 | 1.002 |
| read citm_catalog | 1.000 | 1.001 |
| read canada | 0.993 | 0.997 |
| stream citm_catalog | 1.000 | 1.003 |

With GCC, removing the check costs up to 0.4 % on the rows without number arrays. That's within noise and less than it gains on canada with clang, so the simpler code wins.

*(Written by Claude Code on behalf of @nlohmann.)*
Why is this a false positive?  Isn't it accurate?  Would it not be flagged if the init were `false` instead?

Right, it isn't a false positive. The store is dead: every case that reaches `if (!accepted)` assigns `accepted`, and the only path that doesn't (`default:` for a non-scalar) returns first. An initializer of `false` would be flagged the same way, since DEAD_STORE is about a value that is never read, whatever the value is. The initializer is there for clang-tidy: `.clang-tidy` enables `*`, so `cppcoreguidelines-init-variables` flags an uninitialized local. The suppression stays, but the comment was wrong. `c7de1d7fe0` now says why the store is kept, and `72dbdb2330` does the same in the MessagePack run on #5980.

*(Written by Claude Code on behalf of @nlohmann.)*
I'm surprised that it flags `accepted = true` but not `size = 0`.

Good catch, and it means my last reply was wrong: `false` would not have been flagged. Infer treats a dead store of 0 as an intentional default value and doesn't report it. In the v1.3.0 source, `--liveness-ignored-constant` defaults to `["0"]` (`infer/src/base/Config.ml`), and `is_sentinel_exp` in `infer/src/checkers/liveness.ml` skips stores of those constants, with `int i = 0; if (...) { i = ... } else { i = ... }` as the example. The clang frontend turns `true` and `false` into the integers 1 and 0 (`booleanValue_trans` in `infer/src/clang/cTrans.ml`). So `size = 0` is just as dead as `accepted = true`, but only the store of 1 was reported.

So `85dcd8d0ec` starts `accepted` at `false` and drops the suppression and its comment, and `a6fbdacbf1` does the same in the MessagePack run on #5980. The initializer still satisfies clang-tidy's `cppcoreguidelines-init-variables`.

*(Written by Claude Code on behalf of @nlohmann.)*

title: CBOR reader: read runs of scalar array elements in one loop
